e.t: This word means “anything which is curved” or a “joint.” It is a noun for a bent or connecting part, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, at Exodus 26:17. Its basic meaning points to something shaped with a curve or serving as a point of connection. The precise force of the term in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the object involved.

Adai is a proper name, identified also as “Athe,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:18. Because the available wording gives the name but not the verse text or surrounding context, its specific identity and significance must be determined from that passage itself. Here, the lexical sense is simply the personal name Adai.

Athersatha is a proper name: it identifies someone or something called Athersatha rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. In the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX word, it appears twice, once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. The available lexical meaning is limited to the name itself, so its precise identity and role must be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

This verb means to charge or accuse someone, presenting that person as responsible for a wrong. It describes an act of making an allegation rather than merely noticing or discussing a fault. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, so it is an uncommon word in this corpus. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on who is making the charge and what is being alleged.

Alaōth, also known as Alaoth, is a proper name. It identifies a particular person or place rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs once, at Jeremiah 31:5. The available lexical information identifies the word by name but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning. Its significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from a broader common-noun definition.

Amekasis is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament, identifying a particular named referent rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Its lexical gloss is simply “Amekasis,” so no broader meaning is established here. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Joshua 18:21. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify exactly what Amekasis names there.

Amora is a proper name, rendered as “Amōra” or “Amora.” It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but a specific name used in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Judges 7:1. The name itself does not identify whether the referent is a person or a place; that must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun means “resurrection,” referring to being raised from death to life. It names the event or hope of resurrection rather than describing a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs six times, including passages in Psalms, Daniel, Zephaniah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains resurrection.

This verb means to become deaf—to lose or lack the ability to hear. It describes a change into a condition of deafness rather than simply naming a deaf person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Ezekiel and Micah. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the same: becoming unable to hear. The word appears in Ezekiel 3:26, Ezekiel 24:27, and Micah 7:16.

Arath is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. In the Greek LXX text, it appears once, in Joshua 12:14. The available lexical definition is simply “Arath,” so Scripture does not provide a broader ordinary meaning for this word. Its precise significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and context.

This noun refers to an instrument used for setting or arranging limbs, likely in a medical or surgical setting. Its meaning is specific rather than general: it names a tool employed when a limb needs to be put into proper position. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 4 Maccabees, at 8:13 and 10:5. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain exactly how the instrument is being mentioned in either passage.

Archōb, also rendered Arkhov, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 19:30, identifying a person or place named in that passage. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific referent cannot be clarified further. Its basic function is simply to identify Archōb within the account.

Aseron is a proper name, preserved in English as “Aseron.” It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a broader meaning, but as the name of a particular person or place identified by the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:25. The available word-level information identifies the name itself, while the verse context would be needed to determine whether Aseron names a person, settlement, or another specific entity.

Assathon is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears two times, in 1 Chronicles 4:11 and 4:12. The available lexical information gives the name as “Assathōn” or “Assathon,” but does not provide a further meaning or description of the person. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s place in that genealogy.

Aschanaz is a proper name, referring to a named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. It is rendered “Aschanaz” and does not function as a general description, action, or quality. The name occurs twice in this LXX corpus: once in Genesis 10:3 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:6. Because the available material supplies the name and references but not the surrounding verse text, its specific family or genealogical role must be understood from those passages themselves.

Achelgai, also rendered Akhelye, is a proper name identifying a place or location. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 21:11. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name itself does not provide a broader description, action, or spiritual idea. Its precise significance in that passage comes from the surrounding account, while its lexical function is simply to designate a named place or locality.

Baithsarisa, also rendered Vethsarisa, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific place or named location in the Greek Old Testament, though the available information does not establish further details about that location. This name occurs once in the Greek text, at 2 Kings 4:42. Its precise significance there comes from the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “abominate” and describes treating something as loathsome or deeply detestable. It expresses strong rejection rather than mild dislike. In the Septuagint, it is used 47 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing a recurring way to describe what people or God regard as repulsive and unacceptable. Its exact force in any passage depends on what is being rejected, but the central idea remains intense loathing or abhorrence.

“Gabērōth-chamaam” or “Gaviroth-khamaam” is a proper name identifying a named person or place rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in Jeremiah 48:17. The available lexical information preserves the name in these closely related forms but does not provide a further ordinary-language definition. Its precise identification and significance depend on the surrounding passage and the person or location named there.

This word is a proper name: “Gaidad,” also given as “Yethath.” It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the Greek text, both within Genesis 4:18. Since it is a personal name, its meaning here is primarily identification—the name of the individual mentioned in that passage—not a general word to apply to other people or situations.

Gebeelan is a proper name, rendered in the lexical definition as “Gebeelan” and “Yeveelan.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing a general idea, action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:44. The available information establishes its name and usage as a proper noun, but the surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what the name identifies in that passage.

Godolias is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. The same name may also appear as Gotholias. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 26 times across 25 verses, chiefly in Jeremiah, and also in 2 Kings and Zephaniah. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding account of the person who bears the name.

This word means “tithe,” referring to a tenth portion set apart in biblical giving. It functions as a descriptive word for that portion or offering, rather than naming a person or place. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs 28 times, showing a recurring term for this designated share. Its earliest listed occurrence is Genesis 14:20, and it continues through 1 Maccabees 3:49. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject.

This adjective means “public,” describing something open to or associated with the people generally rather than private or restricted. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains straightforward: it identifies something intended for, visible to, or connected with the public. The surrounding verse determines the exact thing being described, but the word itself points to a public setting, action, or matter.

This word means “lesson”—something taught for instruction or learning. As a noun, it refers to the content or result of teaching rather than the act of teaching itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalms 59:1, but the available verse information does not provide enough context to describe the specific lesson intended there. Its basic sense remains a taught instruction or lesson, with the surrounding passage determining its precise force in that occurrence.

This proper name refers to Dionysos, also rendered Thionisos. It functions as a personal name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. The supplied lexical meaning identifies the name itself, while the exact significance of each occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to a “fifty dollar coin” or “drachma,” a unit of money. It names a coin or monetary amount rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact value or use in a particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “ground,” referring to the earth or a physical surface. It can describe the ground beneath someone’s feet, the surface of a room or building, or earth viewed as a place or material. The word occurs 19 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages connected with the tabernacle, temple construction, worship, and the earth. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on what physical surface or area the surrounding passage identifies.

This Greek LXX verb means “force out”: it describes driving or compelling someone or something out rather than allowing it to remain. As a verb, it expresses an action imposed from outside, so the emphasis falls on expulsion or being made to leave. It occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, each in a different verse. The precise force in any one passage depends on its surrounding wording.

This adjective means “pitiful,” describing someone or something that arouses pity or compassion. It presents its subject as being in a pitiable condition rather than expressing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Daniel, so its meaning is supported by a small number of uses. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word is the personal name “Elisabet,” also given as “Elisavet.” It functions as a proper name rather than a general description, title, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, at Exodus 6:23. The available lexical meaning identifies the name itself, while the reference locates its single occurrence. Its significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named there.

This Greek LXX verb means “set oneself against” or “oppose.” It describes taking a position against someone or something rather than agreeing with or supporting it. As a verb, it expresses active resistance or opposition. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once each in Proverbs, Wisdom, 3 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on whom or what the subject is opposing, but its central idea remains deliberate opposition.

This Greek LXX verb means “lift out/up; remove.” It describes taking something away or lifting it from one place, and its exact force is shaped by the sentence where it appears. It occurs 207 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, so it can describe removal in many settings rather than one narrow action. The word appears especially often in Numbers, Ezekiel, and 1 Maccabees. Its central idea remains a directed taking up or taking away.

This verb means to explore or trace something carefully, suggesting a deliberate search that follows a matter closely. It can describe investigating what is hidden, examining something thoroughly, or tracing its course. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 18 times, so its basic idea is broad enough for searching out people, matters, or the workings of God. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls more on exploring or on tracing, but both meanings involve careful pursuit rather than a quick or casual look.

This verb means “join at top,” describing the act of connecting or bringing something together at its upper end. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:32. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the word itself centers on joining something at the top or upper point.

This adjective describes strong wants or cravings—something intensely desired. It points to the quality of being sought after or longed for, rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Wisdom writings, it occurs three times, so its meaning is focused and consistent rather than broad or common. The simple idea is desire that powerfully attracts someone’s attention. The surrounding verse determines whether the desired thing is presented positively, negatively, or simply as an object of longing.

This LXX verb means “continue; stay on,” describing remaining in a place or situation rather than leaving. As a verb, it expresses ongoing presence or persistence. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Exodus 12:39. The word’s basic sense is therefore to remain or carry on, while the surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on staying in place, continuing an action, or enduring through a circumstance.

This noun means “value” or “price,” referring to what something is worth or what must be paid for it. It expresses an amount or assessment rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 9:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic sense remains the worth or cost assigned to a person or thing.

This word is a proper name rendered as “Euan” or “Evan.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object, so its main function is simply personal identification. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis chapter 4, at Genesis 4:1 and Genesis 4:25. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the individual reference in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX verb means to visit someone or to go around from place to place, making a round of visits. It describes active movement through several places or people rather than simply remaining in one location. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings preserved in the LXX corpus: once in Deuteronomy and once each in 1 and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on whom the person visits and why.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Zembran” or “Zemvran.” It is not a general description or action word, but a personal designation in the Greek Old Testament translation. The name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 1:32. Because no verse text or wider context is provided here, its lexical meaning is the name itself rather than a further description of the person or his role.

“Our” is a pronoun that expresses belonging to, association with, or connection to the speaker together with others. It points to something shared by that group, such as something belonging to them or connected with them. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, this word appears 1,202 times, showing its ordinary use in describing shared possession, identity, or relationship. Its exact reference—who the group includes and what belongs to them—comes from the surrounding sentence.

Thamana is a proper name, functioning as the designation of a particular named subject rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 1:51. The available word-level information identifies the name itself but does not provide the verse text or enough surrounding context to determine whether Thamana refers to a person, place, or another named subject. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the passage context.

To observe means to look at or watch something attentively. This Greek LXX verb describes the act of taking notice of what is before someone, rather than naming a person, object, or abstract quality. It occurs 44 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, making it a recurring word for watching in varied passages. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being observed and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means to “become like a wild beast.” It describes a change into a beast-like state or manner, rather than simply naming an animal. As a verb, it expresses what someone becomes or how someone comes to act. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:11. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning is the movement toward a wild-beast-like condition.

This word is a proper name, identified in the Greek Old Testament as “Iairou; Ieru.” It functions as a personal name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the LXX text, it occurs twice, both times in Esther: once in Esther 1:1 and again in Esther 2:5. These references locate the name, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role in each passage.

Iethnouēl, also rendered Iethnoil, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not presented here as a general term describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 26:2. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional definition or explanation of its parts. Its precise significance in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage and the person being named.

Iescha, also rendered Ieskha, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a woman named in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis 11:29. Because it is a proper name, its main function is to identify the person who bears it, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about her place in the family narrative.

This word is a proper personal name, rendered as “Iōannēn” or “Ioannin.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. Within the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 1 Maccabees. The listed occurrences are in 1 Maccabees 9:36, 13:53, 16:2, and 16:19. The precise person identified in each passage must be determined from the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This word describes a person who commits wrongdoing, especially a malefactor or thief. It functions as an adjective, identifying someone by criminal or harmful conduct rather than naming a particular offense. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times across Esther, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its basic sense remains focused on a person who acts wickedly or unlawfully, while the surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on general wrongdoing or theft.

Karee, also rendered Karie, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in 2 Kings and Jeremiah. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide verse text or a further definition, its precise referent must be understood from the surrounding passage in each occurrence. The name appears in 2 Kings 25:23 and several passages in Jeremiah.

This adjective describes something so unreasonable, foolish, or laughable that it appears ridiculous or absurd. It is used to characterize a person, action, claim, or situation rather than to name an object by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Wisdom 17:8. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what is being called ridiculous there, but the word’s basic sense is clear: it marks something as plainly nonsensical or worthy of ridicule.

This Greek LXX verb means to mourn for someone or to bewail them—that is, to express deep grief over a person or loss. It describes an act of lament rather than a mere feeling of sadness. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Exodus 33:4. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning is grieving openly for someone or something. This adjective means “burning” or “scorching,” describing something characterized by intense heat. It functions as a descriptive modifier, helping identify the heat-producing or searing quality of a thing rather than naming an object or action itself. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense is physical and heat-related, while the surrounding verse identifies what is burning or scorching.

This Greek LXX noun means “branch,” referring to a woody shoot or limb growing from a tree or vine. It is used for parts of plants and trees, whether fresh, spreading, or capable of bearing growth. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, with several occurrences in Ezekiel and others in prophetic books. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and imagery.

This verb means to play the cymbals, describing the act of producing music with that instrument. It is a specific action word rather than a general term for singing, praising, or making music. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 12:27. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular setting, but the word itself plainly identifies cymbal playing. Its meaning is therefore concrete and musical: someone is actively using cymbals in a performance or accompaniment.

Laada is a proper name, rendered “Laada” and also associated with the form “Laatha.” It functions as a personal or identifying name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:21. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific identity cannot be determined here, but its lexical role is simply a named designation.

This verb means “go unnoticed” or describe someone as “unaware.” It expresses a lack of awareness: something is not recognized, observed, or noticed, or a person does not realize what has happened. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used as an action or state involving things escaping attention. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Leviticus, Numbers, Job, and Wisdom. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding sentence presents as unnoticed or unaware.

This Greek LXX noun means “bandit”—a person who takes goods or harms others through robbery. It identifies a criminal who preys on people rather than an ordinary traveler, worker, or merchant. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, including passages in Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Obadiah, Sirach, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a bandit or robber.

To winnow means to separate grain from chaff by exposing it to moving air, so the lighter husks are carried away and the useful grain remains. As a verb, it describes the action of sifting or purifying a harvest. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs 17 times, including passages in Ruth, Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Wisdom writings. Its central idea remains the deliberate separation of what is valuable from what is worthless.

This verb means “soften”: to make something less hard, severe, or firm. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 23:16. As a verb, it describes an action or change rather than a person, object, or quality. The word’s precise force in Job depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here; its clear lexical idea is becoming or making something softer.

Machania is a proper name, also rendered “Makhania.” It identifies a named person or entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:8. The available lexical information establishes the name itself, while the surrounding verse would be needed to determine exactly whom or what Machania identifies there.

Merran is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; its role is to identify someone within the passage. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, Merran occurs once, in Baruch 3:23. The name itself supplies no further meaning beyond this personal designation, so understanding the person’s significance requires the surrounding verse and passage. Merran remains a distinct LXX name rather than a general word translated by an ordinary English term.

Adultery means sexual unfaithfulness within marriage—the violation of the marriage covenant by giving sexual intimacy to someone other than one’s spouse. It is a noun naming this wrongful act. In the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish Scriptures represented here, the word appears four times, always with the meaning “adultery.” Its occurrences are found in Jeremiah, Hosea, and Wisdom, showing that the term is used across both prophetic and wisdom writings. The surrounding verse determines how the act is being addressed in each passage.

Naphthō is a proper name, rendered “Naphthō” or “Naftho.” It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament, but the available information does not specify which. This name occurs twice in the Greek translation of Joshua, in Joshua 15:9 and Joshua 18:15. Its meaning is therefore primarily its role as a name rather than a descriptive word with a separate everyday definition.

Nestha is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 24:8. The available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, so it does not establish further details about the person or the role the name has in that verse.

This adjective describes someone or something carrying wood. It identifies a wood-bearer by the load being carried, giving a straightforward description rather than naming a person, place, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 13:31. The word’s precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains clear: carrying wood. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation’s language and context.

This noun refers to reeds used for thatching houses. It names building material—long plant stalks placed over a roof or covering to form shelter. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:2. The reference identifies where the word appears, while its basic meaning remains the roofing reeds themselves. The word therefore points to ordinary household construction rather than to a person, action, or abstract quality.

This noun means “paean” or “battle cry”: a voiced expression used as a rallying cry. In the Greek LXX, it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 15:25. The definition presents the word as naming the cry itself, rather than an action or person. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, its precise force in that passage cannot be stated more narrowly without adding information beyond the word’s established meaning.

gl: anything drawn along the side: a leathern
d: anything drawn along the side: a leathern

e.t: This noun refers to “anything drawn along the side,” described as “a leathern” item. It names a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 35:11. The precise object intended in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to something leathern that is drawn or placed along a side.

Patroklos is a proper name—the personal name of an individual. It does not describe a general quality, action, or object, but identifies someone specifically. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this name occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 8:9. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be explained further. Its central meaning remains the individual name “Patroklos.”

This verb means “drape” or “clothe,” describing the act of putting clothing or a covering around someone or something. It functions as an action word, so it focuses on what is being done rather than naming a garment or person. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 69 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing regular use for clothing or covering. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains placing something around or upon another.

“Grasping” describes someone or something marked by a grasping quality or character. As an adjective, the word characterizes a person or thing rather than naming an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 1:20. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what the adjective describes there, but its basic lexical idea is grasping.

This word means “bird,” referring to a winged creature. It can function as a noun for a bird or as a describing word connected with birds. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it is used 89 times, from Genesis through 4 Maccabees. Its uses include birds in creation and animal classifications, so the central idea remains the ordinary creature rather than a special symbolic meaning. The precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

gl: make credible; confirm the query of sb
d: make credible; confirm the query of sb

e.t: This verb means to make something credible or to confirm another person’s query. It describes giving assurance that a question, request, or claim can be trusted or accepted. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 18:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here, but its basic sense is to establish credibility or confirm what someone has asked.

This noun means “great experience,” referring to deep or extensive experience gained through what a person has encountered. It describes experience as substantial rather than slight or ordinary. In the Greek Old Testament writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Wisdom and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is a wealth of experience.

This adjective means “much-tangled” or “thick-wreathed,” describing something intricately twisted, woven, or intertwined. It can portray an arrangement with many turns or closely connected strands rather than something simple or straight. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX, in Esther, Job, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact image in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something attached to or overlaid upon something else. It points to an added layer or covering that rests on another object, rather than standing alone. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Jeremiah 10:9, so its broader range cannot be established from repeated biblical usage. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is something placed onto or joined with another thing.

This word means “slap,” referring to a blow delivered with the hand. It is a noun, so it names the physical act or its result rather than describing an action as a verb. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Isaiah 50:6. The word itself expresses a direct, physical strike; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand its particular significance there.

This Greek LXX verb means “rescue”: to deliver someone from danger, trouble, or a destructive situation. It describes an act of saving rather than merely offering help or protection. The word appears 175 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so it is a well-established term for deliverance across many settings. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on who is being rescued and from what circumstance, but its central idea remains being brought safely out of peril.

Samegar is a proper name, referring to a particular person in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered as “Samegar” and does not function as a general word describing an object, action, or quality.
